name: CLI
description: The commands `sumi` answers, and what each one is for.

text: No command takes an option of its own.
`-v` and `-h` are the whole of what a flag says here, and everything a run has to say goes to stdout.
What a run answers is one ladder throughout: `0` where it did what it was asked,
`1` where the two sides differ, and `2` where the comparison could not be made —
whatever had to be read first was absent, unreadable, or ambiguous.
Only `verify` has a second side to differ from, so only it answers `1`.

contracts.name: init
contracts.description: Lay down an empty specification to start a reference line from.

text: Lays down what each mechanism starts from under the root: the glossary as a file,
contract and behavior as directories.
What is already there is reported and left alone: a reference line is not a document to be replaced.
$ sumi init
created .spec/glossary.json
created .spec/contract
exists .spec/behavior

contracts.name: render
contracts.description: Render the structured specification into documents a person reads.

text: Writes what the specification means and not what the tool needs in order to find things,
so a marker, the include globs and the words a glossary rejects stay out.
A document is derived, so a run replaces what the last one wrote,
and a specification that is not there is passed over rather than reported.
$ sumi render
rendered docs/glossary.md
rendered docs/contract/cli.md

contracts.name: verify
contracts.description: Verify the source code is aligned with the verifiable specification.

text: Reports the difference and does not decide which side is wrong —
correcting the specification is as valid an outcome as correcting the code.
A finding answers as `path:line`, relative to where the run started.
$ sumi verify
.spec/behavior/verify.json:6 @behavior V-002 is claimed nowhere in test/*_test.rb
app/order.rb:2 Order rejects Purchase: Order is what the domain calls it.
2 differences

contracts.name: help
contracts.description: Explain how to write a specification, without a document beside the executable.

text: A project using sumi has the command and nothing else of this repository,
and a form it cannot look up is one it guesses at.
Given no topic it lists the commands and the topics; the sections below say what each topic covers,
and the command itself has the form.

contracts.name: help glossary
contracts.description: The vocabulary a project means to use, and the words it rejects.

text: One file at the root of the specification.
An entry names a subdomain, or names none and carries Global; either scopes its terms by include globs,
and a file takes every entry covering it in the order they are written, so Global is written first.
Only the words a term rejects are checked:
a term rejecting none is vocabulary the tool carries but cannot verify.
A rejection carries the places it is wrong, each with the reason that line is right;
the line moving is what makes the run stop and ask again, which a fingerprint would be built to avoid.
"glossary": [
"name": "",
"include": [],
"terms": [
{ "term": "", "definition": "", "not": [
{ "term": "", "reason": "", "ignore": [{ "at": "", "reason": "" }] }

contracts.name: help contract
contracts.description: The interfaces a project means to keep, and the two readings of them.

text: One file per kind of interface, under `contract/`.
Whether a file names a `marker` decides how the source is read: with one, source claims each interface
in the comment in front of the code implementing it; without one, the interfaces are read from the syntax tree
and the file says which `language` spells the names.
One of the two has to be there and never both, so a file taking the second reading
writes `language` where the shape below writes `marker`.
"name": "",
"description": "",
"marker": "",
"include": [],
"contracts": [
{ "name": "", "description": "", "internal": false, "params": [], "notes": [] }
"notes": []

contracts.name: help behavior
contracts.description: The behaviors a project means its tests to implement.

text: One file per feature, under `behavior/`, each carrying its own include.
A scenario is a list of `given` and one sentence each for `when` and `then`, under an id unique across the directory;
test code claims one in the comment in front of the code implementing it.
"name": "",
"description": "",
"include": [],
"scenarios": [
"notes": []

contracts.name: help config
contracts.description: Where the specifications live, what a run touches, and what it answers.

text: `.sumi.json` says where the specifications live, where the documents go,
and which of them a run verifies or renders.
A run reads the nearest one at or above where it started, and a project that has said nothing gets the defaults.
"root": ".spec",
"docs": "docs",
"specifications": { "glossary": { "verify": false, "render": false } }
